summary: Collects the most critical operational considerations for deploying BGP origin validation based on RPKI. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: Advice for checking a route comes from the real owner.

questions: what is a roa max length
subtitle: Practical operating advice for networks that check who is allowed to originate a BGP route, using RPKI data.

tldr.problem: Checking BGP route origins against the RPKI raises many operational questions: where to run caches, how to set routing policy, how to issue ROAs without breaking customers.
tldr.mechanism: This Best Current Practice collects the most critical considerations: run hierarchic repositories and nearby redundant caches, issue precise ROAs, validate only at border routers, and prefer Valid over NotFound over Invalid announcements.
tldr.outcome: It is a living collection of advice rather than a protocol. It warns that origin validation only catches inadvertent mistakes, not malicious spoofing, and it has not been obsoleted or updated.

facts.label: Cache sync interval
facts.value: At least every four to six hours

today: RFC 7115 is a Best Current Practice, published in January 2014, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. The RFC itself says it is expected to evolve as RPKI-based origin validation continues to be deployed.

sections.title: Why Operations Need Advice
sections.content:
RPKI-based origin validation relies on the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI, see RFC 6480). The RFC says that how the RPKI is distributed and maintained globally is a serious concern from many aspects. It notes that the global RPKI was then in early deployment, with no single root trust anchor, and expects that eventually there must be one for the public address space.

Origin validation needs to be done only by an AS's border routers. It is designed to protect announcements originated by any participating network, from large providers to small stub or enterprise networks, and to run on current routers without significant hardware upgrades. With prudent local routing policies, the RFC says, there is little risk that normal routing is threatened by imprudent deployment.

The reader is assumed to know BGP (RFC 4271), the RPKI, Route Origin Authorizations (RFC 6482), the RPKI to Router protocol (RFC 6810) and prefix validation (RFC 6811).
sections.plainLanguage: Checking that a route comes from its real owner is a good idea, but you have to set it up carefully. This document is the list of tips for doing that.

sections.title: Caches, Repositories and Redundancy
sections.content:
The RPKI is a distributed database of certificates, CRLs, manifests, ROAs and Ghostbusters Records. Publishing parties MUST implement hierarchic directory structures, because that improves the performance of relying parties. A relying party can gather a valid cache with rsync and a validation tool, and validated caches may also be built from other validated caches. Operators SHOULD use this to minimize load on the global database, though recipients should re-validate the data.

Routers do not validate cryptographically. Under the RPKI to Router protocol the router trusts its cache and relies on transport security, so the cache data must be well protected. Operators MUST NOT use insecure transports between their routers and RPKI caches located in other Autonomous Systems.

Caches should sit close to the routers that need them, and a router should bootstrap from a cache reachable with minimal reliance on DNS or routing protocols. For redundancy a router should peer with more than one cache, at least one local and others remote. Operators may trust caches offered by their upstreams, which places an obligation on those upstreams to keep them fresh and reliable. Trust Anchor Locators are critical to the trust model, so operators should choose and maintain them with great care.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep a few copies of the official list in different places nearby, so one broken copy does not stop you. Only trust copies you can reach safely.

sections.title: Issuing ROAs Safely
sections.content:
Before issuing a ROA for a super-block, an operator MUST make sure all sub-allocations announced by other ASes, such as customers, already have correct ROAs. Otherwise those sub-allocations will be seen as Invalid. While waiting, the owner may use live BGP data as a proxy to populate ROAs and then safely issue the super-block ROA.

ROAs should be as precise as possible and match the prefixes as announced in BGP. Software and operators SHOULD avoid excessive max length values unless operationally necessary, and ROA generation software MUST use the prefix length as the max length if the user does not specify one. The RFC's reason is that a forged-origin attack cannot succeed against sub-prefixes that an overly long max length would otherwise cover. Issuing 10.0.0.0/16 and 10.0.42.0/24 is better than one ROA for 10.0.0.0/16-24, because an attacker must then go after the whole /16, which is more likely to be noticed.

If a prefix is legitimately announced by more than one AS, ROAs for all of them SHOULD be issued. Operators SHOULD offer to provision RPKI data for customers who do not want to manage certificates and ROAs. They should also use tools that warn of impending ROA or certificate expiry.
sections.plainLanguage: When you write the official list, name exactly who may use each address and nothing more. A list that says too much gives a sneaky person extra room to pretend.

sections.title: Routing Policy and Validity States
sections.content:
Origin validation marks each received announcement as Valid, NotFound or Invalid (RFC 6811). What to do with that mark is up to the operator's local policy. Validation need only be done by edge routers, those bordering other ASes, and policy should fit the AS's existing preferences so that border routers can be upgraded incrementally. As with any policy change, it can cause traffic shifts.

The recommended order is: Valid preferred over NotFound, NotFound preferred over Invalid. Because coverage will be incomplete for a long time, routing on NotFound SHOULD be done for a long time. Announcements with Invalid origins SHOULD NOT be used, though they may be used for special operational needs at a lower preference. The RFC warns that merely de-preferencing Invalid announcements is ill-advised: with longest-match forwarding, a more specific Invalid announcement still attracts traffic whatever its local preference.

Routers implementing origin validation MUST let operators map the validation result to a BGP attribute evaluated after AS_PATH, for providers who do not want it to outrank AS_PATH length. When Local-Preference carries both validity and traffic engineering, do not encode validation state in higher bits than the TE bits, and peer community signaling SHOULD NOT upgrade an Invalid announcement to Valid or better. Validity state signaling SHOULD NOT be accepted from a neighbor AS, since validity has only local scope. When first deploying, it may be prudent not to drop Invalid announcements until logs, SNMP or other data show the right result would be obtained.
sections.plainLanguage: Give the best seats to routes with a stamp, the middle seats to routes with no stamp yet, and keep routes with a wrong stamp out. Merely putting them at the back still lets them in.

sections.title: Notes and Recommendations
sections.content:
The global RPKI is, like the DNS, only a loosely consistent view. Caches are loosely synchronized even within one AS, and there is no guaranteed interval between a cache update and routers learning it. This may cause sudden traffic shifts until all routers reach equilibrium. An operator may choose any polling frequency, but if RPKI data feeds operational routing decisions, local caches inside the AS SHOULD be synchronized with each other at least every four to six hours.

Other points include: associating Ghostbusters Records (RFC 6493) with each publication point an operator controls; supporting four-octet AS numbers on validating routers, since it is not reasonable to generate ROAs for AS 23456 (RFC 6793); and the uncertainty over the origin AS of aggregates, whose long-range solution is the deprecation of AS_SETs (RFC 6472).

Because routers evaluate time-dependent certificates and ROAs, router clocks MUST be correct to a tolerance of approximately an hour, and servers should provide time service such as NTPv4 (RFC 5905). There is also a trade-off in placing an RPKI repository inside the address space it is authoritative for: more control, but harder for others to fix if that space becomes unreachable.
sections.plainLanguage: Different copies of the list may be a little out of date at the same moment, and clocks must be about right, so keep things in sync and watch for surprises.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The BGP origin AS of an update is not signed, so origin validation is open to malicious spoofing. It is therefore expected to deal only with inadvertent mis-advertisement.

It also does not address AS_PATH validation, so paths remain open to manipulation, malicious or accidental. And because BGP does not ensure that traffic flows via the paths it advertises, the data plane may not follow the control plane. Finally, readers are pointed to the privilege escalation issues discussed under routing policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The check catches honest mistakes, not clever liars. A determined cheater can still pretend, so do not treat it as a lock on the door.

items.label: NotFound
items.desc: Still used, at a lower preference than Valid, for a long time.

items.label: Invalid
items.desc: SHOULD NOT be used; if used for special needs, at a lower preference than Valid or NotFound.
